title: Safe and verified Gomory mixed-integer cuts in a rational mixed-integer program framework
contribution: Numerically safe Gomory mixed-integer cuts for exact rational MIP (safe aggregation and MIR by directed rounding for rational data, scaling and denominator control) with VIPR verification through a weak-domination extension completed outside the checker; 21.5% more MIPLIB 2017 runs solved and 26.8% less time in exact SCIP.
problem_entry: Cut separation was the key component still missing from exact SCIP after the status update, and exact GMI cuts would need an exact tableau row and an exact LP (pp. 2–3, 6).
key_idea: Carry the Cook–Dash–Fukasawa–Goycoolea safe GMI cuts into the rational framework: floating-point multipliers, directed-rounding MIR, relaxation of non-representable data, scaling and bounded denominators, VIPR certificates (pp. 3, 5–8, 10–20).
assumptions: Rational MIP min{cᵀx : Ax ≤ b, ℓ ≤ x ≤ u, x_j ∈ Z}; Assumption 1: each variable in a cut has a finite lower or upper bound (held after presolve); IEEE doubles; MIPLIB 2017 benchmark restricted to 132 instances solved by floating-point SCIP 8.0 in 2 h, × 3 seeds (pp. 4, 6, 21).
proof_devices: Safe-rounding device (shift to non-negative space, round in the safe direction, shift back, round the right-hand side up) proving Lemma 1, Corollary 2 and Lemma 3 (pp. 7–8, 10)
Directed-rounding operators per arithmetic operation, Definition 1 (pp. 6–7)
Best rational approximation with bounded denominator via convergents and intermediate fractions, Lemma 4 and Algorithms 1–2 (pp. 12–15); new proof of Lemma 7 (pp. 14, 28–29)
Encoding-length control motivated by the iterative-refinement convergence bound [18, Lemma 5] (p. 11)
MIR validity as a split disjunction plus two aggregations for VIPR, Lemma 5 and Theorem 6 (p. 17)
Weak domination (Definition 2) completed a posteriori by viprcomp (p. 18); exact slack coefficients only for LP-entering cuts (p. 19); optional exact-LP completion (pp. 19–20)
experiments: Five settings (nocuts, safegmi, densmall with denominators ≤ 2^17, fpnocuts and fpgmi with features absent from exact SCIP disabled); MIPLIB 2017 benchmark 132 × 3 seeds, 7200 s, Xeon Gold 5122, SoPlex 6.0.2, PaPILO 2.0.1; shifted geometric means (1 s, 100 nodes); gap closed on 367 runs excluding floating-point/exact disagreements; solved 130/152/158, densmall −26.8% time; fpgmi +39 solved, −35.1% time; certificate overhead +47.1% solving, +57.7% total on 49 instances with one seed; losses from exact-LP spikes reported (pp. 20–26).
positioning: Generalizes Cook, Dash, Fukasawa and Goycoolea (2009) from a floating-point solver to exact MIP; continues Cook, Koch, Steffy and Wolter (2013) and the status update; certification placed beside SAT, pseudo-Boolean and MaxSAT proof logging and the TSP certificate, overhead contrasted with certified pseudo-Boolean symmetry breaking (pp. 2–3, 25–26).
writing: Numbered contributions (p. 3) and three numbered questions (p. 20); light hedging ('hopefully', 'We conjecture', 'reasonably confident', pp. 8, 26–27); differences of gap-closed fractions printed as %, one pair in reverse order (pp. 21–22).
limits_future: Gain smaller than in floating point; exact LP solving is the bottleneck; presolve not certified (pp. 23–26). Future: precision boosting in iterative refinement, separation tuned for exact mode, knapsack cover, flow cover and zero-half cuts (pp. 26–27).

We identify exact LP solving as the main difficulty in making safe cutting planes performant, and show ways to overcome this difficulty by post-processing their coefficients.

title: Certifying MIP-Based Presolve Reductions for 0-1 Integer Linear Programs
contribution: Certifies PaPILO's presolve reductions on 0–1 ILPs with VeriPB pseudo-Boolean proof logging plus a new objective-update rule; proof-logging overhead stays below 6% and verification takes 14.7–22.4 times the presolve time on average.
problem_entry: No methodology exists to certify that a presolved MIP is equivalent to the original; VIPR covers only feasibility-based reasoning, so exact-MIP certificates assume that presolve was valid (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Express each primal reduction by cutting planes or RUP and each dual reduction by redundance-based strengthening with a witness substitution, remove constraints by checked deletion, and add an objective-update rule to VeriPB (pp. 3–11).
assumptions: 0–1 ILPs with integer coefficients (decision and optimization); primal, weak dual and strong dual reductions; invariant: the core set keeps the optimal value; PB10–PB16 and MIPLIB 2017 in OPB translation minus 10 instances at PaPILO's memory limit (pp. 3, 5–6, 12, 15).
proof_devices: VeriPB cutting planes, RUP, redundance-based strengthening with a witness substitution, checked deletion (pp. 3–4)
New objective-update rule: replace f by f′ after deriving f ≥ f′ and f′ ≥ f from the core set; soundness proof omitted (pp. 4–5)
Aggregation with the rational scale split into integer factors s_E/s_D, stored by the presolver (p. 6)
Checked deletion by inverting the replacing derivation (pp. 6–7)

Per-technique recipes: bound strengthening, parallel rows, probing, simple probing, sparsify, coefficient tightening via saturation, GCD simplification via weakening, implied free substitution with witnesses, singleton variables (pp. 7–9)
Dual reductions: duality-based fixing witness, dominated-variable swap witness, four advanced fixings (pp. 9–11)
Worked certificate for an implied free variable, Fig. 1 (p. 11)
experiments: PaPILO 2.2.0 on 6 threads, VeriPB 2.0, Core i5-1145G7 with 16 GB, 3 h, shifted geometric means with shift 1 s; logging overhead below 6% (Table 2); objective differences against full objectives on one instance 3.3 s against 6625 s and 138 GB (other hardware); verification 14.7–22.4 times generation, 25% of instances at least 193 times, 38 timeouts scored PAR2 (Table 3); RUP against explicit POL proofs: POL 0.7–13.1% faster, RUP recommended (Table 4); stated totals 671/1681 do not match Table 2 sizes (my arithmetic); single runs (pp. 12–15).
positioning: Sets MIP against SAT's proof logging (DRAT, GRIT, LRAT); states the limits of VIPR; claims the first use of VeriPB for reformulations of optimization problems; reads overhead against certified CNF translations; presolve methods from Achterberg et al. 2019, Savelsbergh, Gamrath et al., Gemander et al. and PaPILO (pp. 2, 6–10, 13).
writing: 'First step' framing; experimental findings offered as input for revising the proof format; a surprise reported and then explained; confident close ('we believe our results show convincingly') (pp. 1–2, 14–15).
limits_future: 0–1 ILPs only; the objective-update rule is not proven in the paper; verbose certificates and heavy verification on a quarter of the instances. Future: native substitution rule (up to 90% smaller certificates), ordered RUP hints, bounded and unbounded integer and continuous domains via [34, 42] and the proof system [20] (pp. 3, 5, 13, 15).

title: The MIP Workshop 2023 Computational Competition on reoptimization
contribution: Designs the MIPcc23 reoptimization competition: twelve public and hidden series of 50 related MILPs, public generation scripts, sequential rules and a banded, position-weighted score; reports the winner and an honourable mention without a score table.
problem_entry: MILP benchmarks solve instances from scratch, while practice and decomposition algorithms solve series of similar instances; no reoptimization benchmark exists (pp. 1–3).
key_idea: Series of 50 related instances solved in order using only information from earlier ones; a banded per-instance score, per-instance ranks and higher weights for later instances; no offline training (pp. 2, 6–7).
assumptions: MILP series with fixed dimensions in which objective, bounds, sides or matrix vary; 7 public and 5 hidden constant-matrix series, 3 matrix-varying series outside the evaluation; bases from MIPLIB, stochastic programs, column generation, hydro unit commitment, vaccine allocation with big-M and an SAP supply chain; limits 60–600 s (pp. 2–5).
proof_devices: n/a for proofs; design devices of the instrument follow
Selection of 50 instances by from-scratch solve time and cosine similarity of the varying vector (p. 3)
Score f = reltime + gap + nofeas with bands [0, 1], [1, 2] and 3, continuous at the band boundary (pp. 6–7)
Loophole rules: reltime above 1 past the limit, reltime = 1 for early stops without zero gap (p. 7)
Twice the worst possible rank for infeasible solutions or invalid dual bounds (p. 7)
Final score C = Σ_s Σ_i (1 + 0.1 i) r(s, i) (p. 7)
Rules: sequential order, no look-ahead, no later change of answers, 1 thread, 16 GB (p. 6)
experiments: none as an experiment: no scores, ranks or baselines printed; twelve registrations, six submissions, winner Patel (SCIP-based reuse of primal information and pseudocosts, online tuning), honourable mention Strang et al. (influence branching); the from-scratch solver, the validity check, the hardware and the weighting of the jury's criteria are not stated (pp. 3, 6–7).
positioning: Claims the first dedicated reoptimization benchmark; earlier reoptimization work cited as application-specific or limited; the score is set against measures such as the confined primal integral (pp. 2–3, 6).
writing: A design report giving a reason for each rule and score term; one self-assessment without evidence ('In our mind, this scoring framework allows for nuanced evaluation') (pp. 6–7).
limits_future: Matrix-changing series not evaluated; nothing in the paper to reproduce the ranking from. Future: grow the generation scripts into a reoptimization benchmark library and add series (pp. 2, 7).

coauthors: Suresh Bolusani, Mathieu Besançon, Timo Berthold, Claudia D'Ambrosio, Gonzalo Muñoz, Joseph Paat, Dimitri Thomopulos

quotes.text: The intention of this competition was not to perform offline training on different types of applications but to reuse information from current and previous solving processes to accelerate the solution of future instances.
we also aimed to avoid unduly restricting approaches that engage in an early exploration phase, which might intentionally deteriorate performance for the first few instances of a series.

title: Certified Constraint Propagation and Dual Proof Analysis in a Numerically Exact MIP Solver
contribution: Numerically safe constraint propagation and dual proof analysis in exact SCIP with VIPR certification of the derived bounds, cutting time by 23.4% and nodes by 28.9% and solving 15 more of 396 MIPLIB 2017 runs.
problem_entry: Propagation and conflict analysis had not been adapted to exact MIP; earlier exact-MIP work shows numerical techniques must run in floating point in a numerically safe way (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Keep floating-point propagation and dual proof analysis, but maintain activities and aggregate conflict rows with directed rounding, take dual rays from the floating-point LP, and certify bounds by VIPR linear combinations plus a repair step (pp. 5–8).
assumptions: MIP min cᵀx s.t. Ax ≥ b with bounds and integrality; finite bounds for presentation, propagation skipped otherwise; MIPLIB 2017 benchmark restricted to 132 instances solved by floating-point SCIP 8.0.3 in 2 h, × 3 seeds (pp. 3, 9).
proof_devices: Safe activity maintenance by directed rounding, no recomputation needed (p. 6)
Farkas proof and bound-exceeding argument showing that propagation on the conflict constraint cuts off the node (pp. 4–5)
Floating-point dual ray with slightly negative multipliers set to zero, since any conic combination is valid (p. 6)
Sign-of-bounds case rule for safe aggregation (pp. 6–7)
VIPR linear combination with multipliers 1/a_k and a rounding step for propagated bounds, eqs. (6)–(7) (pp. 7–8)
viprcomplete repair of conflict constraints after solving (p. 8)
experiments: SCIP 8.0.3, SoPlex 6.0.3, GMP 6.1.2, PaPILO 2.0.1, Xeon Gold 5122, 2 h, 396 instance-seed runs, shifted geometric means (1 s, 100 nodes); exact: −23.4% time, −28.9% nodes, +15 solved (Table 1); reduced floating-point SCIP: −44.5% time, +31 solved (Table 2); subsets differ between the arms; certificate time excluded and no certificate checked; without propagation time 17.1% and 28.3%; two denominator remedies null; the text's floating-point node reductions (65.1%, 67.1%) do not match Table 2 (38.8%, 42.4%, my arithmetic) (pp. 8–12).
positioning: Continues Cook, Koch, Steffy and Wolter (2013), the Eifler–Gleixner status update and the safe GMI cuts; dual proof analysis from Witzig, Berthold and Heinz; certification framed by certifying algorithms and SAT, SMT, pseudo-Boolean and MIP certification (p. 2).
writing: Third-person abstract; enumerated reasons for the exact–floating-point gap; a null remedy reported with its reading; one unhedged forecast ('is sure to yield positive impact') (pp. 1, 10–12).
limits_future: Smaller gains than in floating point, 'partially the price to be paid for exactness'; exact bound changes are costly; no propagation in strong branching. Future: floating-point bound changes, propagation in strong branching, conflict strengthening from [WBH21], graph-based conflict analysis, recomputed activities (pp. 10–12).

quotes.text: for numerical techniques to be beneficial, it is crucial to employ them as much as possible using floating-point arithmetic in a numerically safe way, as symbolic computation can be prohibitively slow.

Such weaker performance is partially the price to be paid for exactness, coming from weaker inequalities due to directed rounding and the fact that we cannot determine infeasibility within tolerances in the exact setting.

title: Branch and Cut for Partitioning a Graph into a Cycle of Clusters
contribution: A problem-specific binary formulation, polyhedral results, separation of triangle, partition and extended subtour and path inequalities, and four heuristics for cycle clustering, which beat RLT-based branch and cut on 65 biology simulation instances once separation is on.
problem_entry: Cycle clustering of nonreversible Markov state model data has proven hard to solve to global optimality; the generic compact RLT linearization is the competitor (pp. 1–3).
key_idea: Variables only for the same-cluster and consecutive-cluster relations, plus problem-specific separation routines and heuristics in SCIP (pp. 4–9).
assumptions: Complete graph with nonnegative non-symmetric weights, m clusters, objective α·net flow + (1 − α)·coherence; set-partitioning assignment; 65 instances with 20–250 vertices and 3–15 clusters, α = 1/1.001 (pp. 1–3, 9).
proof_devices: Equivalence of RLT and CC solutions and the same root bound via x = 1/m (p. 5)
Polytope dimension and facet results; facet proofs deferred to an extended version (p. 5)
Triangle inequalities, Theorems 1–2, separated by enumeration in O(n³) (p. 6)
Partition inequalities, Theorem 3, heuristic separation with |S| + |T| ≤ 5 (p. 7)
Extended subtour and path inequalities valid by counting forward transitions in multiples of m; exact separation by dynamic programming in O(n³m), Theorem 4 (pp. 7–8)
Heuristics: greedy O(n²m), sparsify sub-MIP, rounding O(nm), Lin–Kernighan exchange with perturbations (pp. 8–9)
experiments: SCIP (version not stated; reference is the SCIP 6.0 report) with default settings plus the new plugins, 7200 s, one job per node, Xeon E5-2670 v2; shifted geometric means (10 s, 100 nodes, 1000 for integrals); CC with separation 31 solved against RLT 29, RLT with separation 28, plain CC 24; separation hurts RLT; component-at-a-time ablation (subtour the best separator, exchange the best heuristic); no seeds; the claim that all heuristics together are best is not matched by Table 2's solved counts (pp. 9–11).
positioning: Linearization lineage Padberg, McCormick, Liberti, Mallach and RLT; inequalities from graph partitioning (Chopra and Rao, Grötschel and Wakabayashi); exchange after Kernighan and Lin; RLT credited with the best out-of-the-box performance (pp. 3, 6–7, 9, 11).
writing: Contribution list by section; hedged explanations ('This may be explained by'); deferred proofs flagged; one summary sentence not matched by its table (pp. 2, 5, 10–11).
limits_future: Only 52.3% of the instances solved by any setting; large final gaps; facet proofs deferred; the plugins stay problem-specific (not the generic-component mark of Research Taste 8); no future work beyond an extended version (pp. 5, 10–11).
